title: Loops: summarising a stream of numbers
summary: Repeat work with while and for: read input until it runs out, compute running statistics, handle the empty case, and nest loops.

steps.title: Read until the input runs out
hints: `std::cin >> value` is itself a condition: it is true when a value was read, false when input ends or isn't a number.

steps.title: Smallest, largest, average — and nothing at all
hints: What should `min` start as? Not 0 — then all-positive input would report min 0. Use the *first* value you read: `if (count == 0 || value < min) min = value;`
Check `count == 0` after the loop and print `no numbers` instead of dividing by zero.

quiz.question: How many times does the body of `for (int i = 1; i < 10; ++i) { ... }` run?
explanations: Count them: i takes the values 1, 2, …, 9. When i becomes 10 the condition `i < 10` is false and the loop stops before running the body.

Right: 1 through 9. A loop `for (int i = a; i < b; ++i)` runs exactly `b - a` times. This *half-open* range [a, b) is the convention everywhere in C++ — indices `0 .. size()-1`, iterators `begin()` to `end()` — precisely because it makes counting easy.
That would need `i <= 10` starting from 0. Off-by-one errors are the most common loop bug; the half-open convention is designed to avoid them.
It is fully defined by the language: initialise once, test the condition before each iteration, run the body, then the increment.

steps.title: Challenge: a multiplication table

expect.contains: n must be a positive whole number

hints: One loop for rows; *inside* it, another loop for columns. After the inner loop finishes, print `'\n'`.
No trailing space: print a space *before* every number except the first in a row (`if (col > 1)`).
